# Page 9^page=9
2. Hardware & Pinout Mapping 02

# Page 10^page=10
10 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Pin assignment The CubeMX interface already maps the pins for the selected NUCLEO board. However, we will need to configure the pins for the POLIMI board ourselves! This information is in the schematics presented in the previous lab.

# Page 11^page=11
11 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Pin assignment Example: driving the Green LED on the NUCLEO Schematic: Pin PA5 is physically connected to the Green LED. CubeMX Action: Left-click on PA5, it is already set as GPIO_Output. Pin multiplexing: a single physical pin can serve multiple purposes. This menu displays all the Alternate Functions available for PB6 (e.g., it can act as an I2C1 SCL line, a USART1 TX line, etc.)

# Page 12^page=12
12 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Pin assignment Best Practice: Right-click on a pin to set a label to the pin and name it to match the schematic.

# Page 13^page=13
13 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Pin assignment Example: Activating a peripheral (e.g., I2C) CubeMX Action: Expand the "Connectivity" menu on the left and enable I2C1 (Set I2C Mode). CubeMX automatically assigns and highlights the default hardware pins for I2C1 (SCL and SDA, which in this case are assigned to PB6 and PB7)

# Page 14^page=14
14 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Pin assignment Reality Check: Do these default pins match our schematic? If our PCB designer used different pins with respect to the default ones, we must remap them in CubeMX to match the ones on the physical board. You can assign the correct pins directly by clicking them, according to your schematic. However, they will turn orange. This is a warning: the pin is reserved, but the actual I2C peripheral is still disabled in the menu!

# Page 15^page=15
15 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Pin assignment CubeMX allows us to configure the peripheral as needed: we will see that each peripheral has different configuration options.

# Page 16^page=16
16 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Try it yourselves! Create a new project and try to look at the various pins and functionalities, so that you get familiar with the interface. In the meantime, we will distribute the boards that will be needed for the next steps. If you had any issues with the set-up, please let us know.

3. Code Generation 03

# Page 18^page=18
18 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code generation 1. Define project name and project location on your PC. 2. Then select Cmake as Toolchain/IDE 3. Click on “Generate Code”

# Page 19^page=19
19 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code generation Tip: save all your projects in a defined folder!

# Page 20^page=20
20 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code generation Open the project folder on Visual Studio Code (VSC) and click on the STM32 Cube extension, then “Set Up STM32Cube project(s)” Check the Board name and click on “configure”

# Page 23^page=23
23 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code generation In the file explorer, you can see the files of the project: - main.c is the file we will mostly edit - Project_name.ioc is the file that CubeMX uses for the GUI - In Inc you will find .h files, containing configurations, etc The main.c file is configured as we discussed in the first class: int main(void) { while (1) { } }

# Page 24^page=24
24 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code generation CubeMX translates our GUI settings into C functions automatically placed in main.c Always write your custom code ONLY between the /* USER CODE BEGIN */ and /* USER CODE END */ comments! If you write outside these blocks, CubeMX will permanently delete your code upon the next generation.

# Page 25^page=25
25 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code generation After clicking on “Run and Debug”, choose “STM32Cube: STM32 Launch STLink GDB Server.” You will need the board to be connected to run and to debug the code.

# Page 26^page=26
4. Debugger 04

# Page 27^page=27
27 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code debug Clicking on the dot next to a line inserts a breakpoint. The code will stop whenever that line is reached: we can then analyze variables, registers, etc to verify our code is working correctly. To proceed with code execution (or to stop it if something is wrong) we can use the dedicated commands. Breakpoint

# Page 28^page=28
28 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code debug Here we can monitor registers and variables. To check a variable’s value, we might need to add it to the «watch» section. We can also add «expressions», to verify if a computation we perform in our code is correct.

# Page 29^page=29
29 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Code debug Example: counter++ increases each time we play the code, which stops at each while cycle execution. When we are done with the debugging phase, we can remove the breakpoints and the code will run smoothly.
